What it is

The paper's story: where it is used, its core idea and the real system demo.
Real-world use

A reflected path into a building

By placing MilliMirror nearby to reflect and refocus the mmWave beam, a strong NLoS path can be createdNLoS means non-line-of-sight. The panel sends the wave around the blocked direct path and through the window.

Open paper ↗ Publisher record ↗
Outdoor-to-indoor link

It shows A layout and panel views redrawn from Fig. 1.

How to read it The solid fan reaches the radio through the window after the dashed paths miss it.

Motivation

Blocked paths limit coverage

  1. 1Due to the blockage of LoS and lack of (or weak) multipaths from natural reflectors
  2. 2smooth concrete reflects signals strongly but only specularly
  3. 3it is questionable whether it will become a scalable solution, considering the high implementation cost
Paths before MilliMirror

It shows A blocked link, a flat wall and a powered relay.

How to read it A blocked direct line of sight (LoS) leaves the radio relying on weak or missing bounces.

State of the art

Simple cells allow a closed-form model

existing RF metasurface elements have complex electromagnetic artifacts such as mutual couplingA formula can give the phase shift from each cell’s depth. With other cell designs, nearby cells can affect that shift.

Cell model and solver benchmark

It shows Runtime bars drawn from Table 1.

How to read it The two-axis fit took 1.82 s, versus 1.51 s for iterative Fourier and 1,220.81 s for the joint autocorrelation fit.

Background

Phase and beam direction

PhaseWave phase

different phase shifts ranging from 0° to 360° can be appliedA different cell depth shifts the phase by a different angle.

Phase tells where a wave is in its cycle.

CellUnit reflector

MilliMirror uses the metal-backed dielectric cuboid (MBDC) as the unit element

A plastic block sits over a thin metal film.

Beam widthAngular span

we represent the objective beam pattern by specifying the direction and width of the beamHere the blind spot can be covered by one main beam.

A wider beam reaches more directions.

Waves leave the cells

It shows A drawing of the angle of each cell’s wave cycle and the beam they form.

How to read it Arrow angles show shifts in the wave cycle, and their difference gives the relative phase.

Core idea

Cell depths set the reflected beam

  1. 1the incidental signals penetrate the dielectric cuboids with different thickness
  2. 2the metasurface can have certain distribution of phase shifts
  3. 3can reflect mmWave signals towards anomalous directions
Cell depth and beam angles

It shows Depth steps under a flat face and the two angles of a beam.

How to read it Depth sets the round trip to the metal backing and thus the phase that steers the combined wave away from the usual mirror direction.

Core idea · what to observe

The beam can leave at a new angle

by controlling the thickness of the MBDCs, the metasurface can have certain distribution of phase shiftsA metal-backed dielectric cuboid (MBDC) is a plastic block with a metal back. It shifts the phase of each reflected wave. Add the waves with their phases and square the resulting amplitude to find the power at each angle.

Angle from panel normal –
Reflected power

It shows The flat plate peaks at its mirror angle of 0°, and the stepped panel gives a stronger return in the shaded target band.

How to read it Read the two curves at the shaded band, using 0° for straight out and dBsm for decibels relative to one square meter.

The real system

Field tests found new radio paths

MilliMirror can effectively fill the coverage holes and operate transparently to the standard mmWave beam management protocolsThe design covers wide bands and panels with thousands of cells. Commercial 60 GHz 802.11ad radios found the panel with the usual scan when the receiver stayed in the fan.

Challenge 1 · Cell phase

Equal cells give equal phase

Equal depths give equal phases, so the beam stays at the flat mirror angle.

the incidental signals penetrate the dielectric cuboids with different thickness

Angle from panel normal –
Flat metal reflection

It shows A wave that hits the plate head on comes straight back at 0°.

How to read it The arrows show reflected waves at four spots on one plate, and the plot uses 0° for straight out.

Solution 1 · Cell phase

Cell thickness sets the phase

MilliMirror uses the metal-backed dielectric cuboid (MBDC) as the unit elementThe wave crosses the plastic, bounces off the metal and crosses it again. Half a wavelength of added depth in the plastic makes one turn. The paper tests vacuum grooves as a separate design.

  1. The metal sits behind the slab.
  2. Compare the phase model with the digitized full-wave points.
  3. Your turn Switch to bare metal and look for the flat phase line.
Phase shift –
Thickness and phase

It shows Half a wavelength in the slab gives a full turn of phase.

How to read it The dot follows the ideal curve, and the blue points come from the paper's full-wave simulation.

Challenge 2 · Lobe nulls

A joint phase fit can leave lobe nulls

minimizing the side lobe level results in nulls in the main lobe regionA null is a weak spot inside the main beam. Reducing power outside that beam can create weak spots inside it. Instead of a search that can settle on a poor fit, the paper fits row and column cuts separately using a slope from autocorrelation and Newton’s method.

RCS at the scan dot –
Joint fit across two axes

It shows The same cell phases shape the beam and cut stray power, so the joint fit can leave dips in the beam.

How to read it The top dot scans outgoing azimuth at 0° tilt, and radar cross section (RCS) shows how strongly the beam scatters there.

Solution 2 · Lobe nulls

Separate axis fits fill the fan beam

A more flat main lobe without nulls is achieved thanks to the flat 1D patterns that are more easily synthesized.A box on the design grid lets the solver fit each axis on its own. Each cell adds its row and column phase shifts.

  1. One target spans both axes.
  2. The rectangular goal allows two fits that multiply to form the map.
  3. Your turn Compare the dips in the 0° tilt cut.
RCS at the scan dot –
Fan beam synthesis

It shows The two fits make the dips in this fan beam less deep.

How to read it Radar cross section (RCS) gives scatter strength at the dot's outgoing azimuth, with tilt at 0°.

Challenge 3 · Beam squint

Beams steered off the mirror angle can shift

the actual beam pattern is distorted when the frequency of the incident signal deviates from the carrier frequency by designPath phase differences between cells on both legs vary with frequency and cancel at the mirror angle. Under normal incidence the incoming leg is equal across cells. The wideband fit takes the union of grid regions for the same desired directions at each frequency.

  1. At lower frequencies the path phases change and the beam can move.
  2. The two path lengths set the phases at each frequency.
Wave frequency –
Beam drift with ideal phase weights

It shows The steered beam drifts off the target as frequency changes, while a plain mirror's return still follows the mirror angle.

How to read it The solid curve uses fixed cell phases even though a real backed cell's phase also shifts with wavelength.

Solution 3 · Beam squint

Band union sustains power at the target

set the main lobe region in the objective pattern as the union of the main lobe regions of all frequencies in the desired working band.A shorter wave fits more cycles between cells, so the same aim maps to a new point on the grid.

  1. One aim maps to different spots on the grid.
  2. The wide goal spans both edges.
  3. Your turn Compare the return at 45° from straight out, with 0° tilt.
Radar cross section at 45° –
A beam across the band

It shows The band fit spreads the beam, raising the edge return at 45° and lowering the peak at 64 GHz.

How to read it The final plot reads the return at 45° azimuth from straight out, with 0° tilt.

Challenge 4 · Print constraints

Printed cells have discrete heights

The thicknesses of MBDCs are quantized with a resolution of 0.1 mmThe authors chose this spacing for PA 12 nylon. Similar fabrication errors preserve relative phase. A thin sputtered seed layer takes the thicker copper coat by plating.

Cell depth minus design –
Print steps and cell phase

It shows Each depth rounds to one print step, which changes that cell's phase.

How to read it The dot tracks one cell's depth from the flat face to its metal back.

Solution 4 · Print constraints

A coated print forms the stepped surface

The thicknesses of MBDCs are quantized with a resolution of 0.1 mm.MBDCs are plastic cells with metal behind them. Chromium sticks to the plastic, and the thin copper coat then carries current to grow the thick copper film.

  1. The print starts with stepped depths.
  2. The 0.4 mm base gives the weakest stray return in the mirror direction.
  3. Your turn Switch print steps off to compare with the design depth.
Cell depth minus design –
Printed depths and metal backing

It shows Copper blocks waves from passing through the printed panel and boosts the reflected wave.

How to read it The final plot scans the fan angle while the cell depth tracks a separate scan along one column.

Check the Paper · 1 of 3

Real-to-Simulation Gap

Field traces include the effects of the radios and the site.The field points come from the paper’s plots. Tilts and warping are possible causes of the power changes in the size test. The ideal model predicts the bounce from the panel.

BeamsSizeChannelsWindowCornerScansBenchSynthesisPrinting

The dashed model trace shows the shape of the 20° fan.The shape view scales the model and the measured 20° fan to their own peaks. The field view keeps the same power scale for all three widths.

Received power near the main beam rose about 3 dB and then 4 dB as the panel area doubled.

The tests compare two panels aimed at 45° on three channels of one 60 GHz radio.The narrowband design fits 60.48 GHz; the wideband fit covers all three centers. The ideal 16 cm reference uses the aperture from the size test. The modeled wideband design keeps more power at 45° on the outer channels, with a lower peak at the center channel.

The panel helped at the window and when the receiver faced away from the sender.

Flat copper gave its strongest return near the center of the receiver line.At +1.6 m, MilliMirror gave −58 dBm and flat copper gave −62 dBm. The tripod trace is the radio link with the reflector removed.

Open the corner model

The radios found the panel’s direction with their usual beam scans.The first scan steers the sender. The second steers the receiver while the original sender records power. Colors show the strength reported at each scan and receiver location.

The authors tested how size, beam width and aim change reflected strength.The paper’s model and full-wave sweeps show size, width and aim. In (d), the design points back toward the sender, away from the ordinary mirror direction.

The synthesis methods distribute power differently across the fan.Fig. 5 shows weak spots within the target beam for Fourier and joint fits. The distributions summarize the sample directions inside and outside the main beam.

The paper tested how printing choices affect reflection.In one full-wave test the panel was designed for permittivity 2.5. The other tests varied cell width or compared dielectric cells with air grooves. Material mismatch and cell width had small effects.

Generalization study

Question Where does the beam peak as fan aim and frequency change?

You change
Fan aim, widths, design band and read frequency
  1. 1Your turn Aim near 75°.The paper’s pencil beam lost about 4 dB at 70° from the panel normal. That gives a span of about ±70° at that loss. This bench keeps cell gain fixed.
  2. 2Your turn Widen the fan to 30°.A broad fan uses the same set of cells. The shade shows the part of the target that fits in the view.
  3. 3Your turn Read past 71 GHz.The cell depths stay fixed as the read frequency changes. The paper chose 57 to 71 GHz for its WiGig example.

Go Beyond the Paper · 2 of 3

Physical conditions

Question Which build changes scatter power away from the aim?

You change
Material, pitch, thinnest layer and space between print heights
  1. 1Your turn Set permittivity to 3.5 to change wavelength and phase delay in the cell.The paper designed for 2.5 and changed the simulated value to test mismatch. Here the design uses the measured PA 12 value of 2.55. The slider changes the value that sets each cell’s phase delay.
  2. 2Your turn Increase the pitch to 2.5 mm.Pitch is the gap between cell centers. Past a quarter wavelength, some angles can share a phase step. The paper kept the panel at 4 × 4 cm. Here the cell count stays fixed, so the panel grows with pitch.
  3. 3Your turn Set the thinnest layer to 1.4 mm.The floor is the least depth needed for strength when printed. A higher floor shifts the whole depth range. The paper’s full-wave test saw a stronger mirror return as its cell model grew less exact. Here phase errors at the band edge can raise that return.
  4. 4Your turn Set print heights 0.4 mm apart.The paper uses 0.1 mm steps. A larger step rounds the cell depths more. Zero keeps them exact.

Limits of this model

What This Model Leaves Open

Not modelled

Shown by the paper, not simulated here.

  1. Curved metal reflector simulationsCurved metal currents need a different electromagnetic model. Fig. 23
  2. Open-field receiver arcField cuts show the receiver angle on the reflector’s 10 m semicircle. Fig. 12(a); §7.2
  3. Airfide antenna selectionTests used all eight 6 × 6 sender arrays and one receiver element. §7.1; Fig. 12(a)
  4. Sender scan angleThe scan is shown from the paper. The radio's antenna weights are needed to model it live. Fig. 17; §7.2
  5. Receiver scan angleThe reverse scan is shown from the paper. The radio's antenna weights are needed to model it live. Fig. 18; §7.2
  6. Cylindrical reflector curvatureThe scale ranges from a flat plate at 0 to a half cylinder at 1. The model uses flat arrays. Fig. 23(a); §8
  7. Cylindrical reflector sizeThe paper varied curved surfaces from 1 to 4 cm. The model solves only flat sheets. Fig. 23(b); §8
  8. Field sitePower at four sites is shown in the evidence. The model leaves out extra signal paths in each room or outdoor site. Fig. 22; §8
  9. Return-to-source incidenceThe evidence shows the paper's incidence sweep. The live slice uses a set incidence for its reflector. Fig. 6(d); §3.3
  10. Small test panel side lengthThe evidence shows the paper's smaller 2–8 cm panels. The layout starts with its larger field samples. Fig. 6(a); §3.3
  11. Manual one-cell depthThe demo automatically sweeps a full phase cycle; the solver sets array depths. Fig. 2(b); §3.1
  12. Printer materialThe model uses the measured PA 12 value. VisiJet M3 and VeroClear were compared for print quality. §5.1
  13. Backing metal thicknessThe build uses the paper's 15 µm copper film. The phase model treats the film as an ideal conductor. §5.2; Fig. 11
  14. Vertical aim of the fanThe main live plot is the horizontal slice of the reflector. The example fan is centered at 0° vertically. §3.2; Fig. 5
  15. Pencil, paired or fan beamsThe evidence shows each field pattern. The adjustable solver starts from a single fan or pencil beam. Figs. 13–14; §7.2
